title: "3.3 Rigid-body acceleration (extra)"

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

Just to wrap up the example I tried to do in class. We'll answer in two ways: mathematically and physically.


::: {.callout-tip}
One nice thing about oral examinations is that we can talk more about the physics and not get lost in the math... though this problem is way tougher than I would ask about in an MCEN 3021 exam!
:::



## The problem

If you've ever tried to hold a drinking vessel in a car or plane you are aware that the vehicle's movement causes sloshing. This sloshing is certainly not "hydrostatic" but we can think about what would happen during steady acceleration, assuming it has reached steady state.

We'll set this up in plain Cartesian coordinates. Gravity acts in the $-\hat{y}$-direction, and the vehicle undergoes constant acceleration in the $+\hat{x}$-direction at acceleration $a$ — pick $\hat x$ to point along the vehicle's direction of travel, so accelerating "forward" means accelerating in $+\hat x$.


The case we started to describe in class, where we move through a large horizontal circle, requires cylindrical coordinates. Too complicated to describe with no preparation, I discovered. This one is just: we are driving in a straight line and accelerating. We still expect the surface of our coffee to shift — now it will "lean" towards us, right?

To orient our coordinate system, imagine you are the passenger in the vehicle looking at the driver holding a cup of coffee. The $+\hat{x}$-direction is to the right (the direction of acceleration) and the $-\hat{y}$-direction is down (the direction of gravity). We expect based on experience that the surface will adopt a shape like $y = - cx$ for some constant $c$. 

## Solution

Revisit the equations we derived right before assuming zero acceleration:

$$
\rho \mathbf{a} = -\boldsymbol{\nabla} p + \rho \mathbf{g}.
$$

We can write these in terms of Cartesian components:

$$
\begin{align*}
    \rho a_x &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\\
    \rho a_y &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}-\rho g\\
    \rho a_z &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}
\end{align*}
$$

and then simplify to the case where we have only $x$-acceleration, $a_x=a$, with $a_y=a_z=0$:

$$
\begin{align*}
    \rho a &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\\
    0 &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}-\rho g\\
    0 &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}.
\end{align*}
$$

We can integrate the first equation to find $p(x,y,z)=-\rho a x + c(y,z)$ where $c(y,z)$ is a "constant of integration"... in principle, this can depend on $y$ and $z$.

::: {.column-margin}
Notice when we take the derivative of this equation with respect to $x$, we end up back with $\partial p/\partial x = -\rho a$.
:::

We can do the same with the second equation, arriving at $p=-\rho g y + d(x)$ where $d(x)$ is a "constant of integration" that can depend on $x$ and $z$. The third equation reveals that $p$ is not a function of $z$ (otherwise $\partial p/\partial z$ would not be zero). We then realize

$$
p(x,y) = -\rho a x - \rho g y ~~+ \text{constant}.
$$


::: {.callout-tip title="Wisdom"}
Now let's make two wise observations: firstly, the constant does not have anything to do with the surface orientation, it is just an offset value, so we can just say it is zero; secondly, the surface will be at zero gauge pressure.
:::

Thus we solve when $p(x,y)=0$ 

$$
0 = -\rho a x - \rho g y \implies y =  -\frac{a}{g} x.
$$

What does this mean? **This is the vertical location of the surface, assuming $y$ increases with altitude.** This is exactly what we expect to occur in our thought experiment: accelerate forward, and the coffee climbs up the back side of the cup.

## Think about it another way

Now that we've solved it out, let's figure out how to talk about it more intuitively.

Going back to our second piece of wisdom, the surface is at constant pressure, $p(x,y)=0$. **This tells us that the pressure gradient is perpendicular to the surface.** So we can go back to

$$
\begin{align*}
    \rho a &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}\\
    0 &= -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}-\rho g
\end{align*}
$$

and realize

$$
\left\langle \frac{\partial p}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}\right\rangle = \rho \left\langle -a , -g \right\rangle.
$$

This is a surface normal pointed toward the back of the vehicle and downwards with gravity — again, exactly what we expect.


## Think about it another way

Can we get away from math entirely? Think about a free body diagram for the coffee (the entirety of the liquid body, which is not changing shape because we are at steady state): gravity acts downwards, and then some force must be applied to cause the fluid's forward ($+\hat x$) acceleration.


::: {.callout-tip title="Wisdom"}
Recall that, when it was just hydrostatics, the pressure gradient acted downwards because gravity acted downwards... the pressure gets higher the deeper you go. Now we have an additional acceleration in the forward ($+\hat x$) direction, and to produce a forward force we need higher pressure pushing from behind — i.e. a larger pressure toward the back of the vehicle... the pressure gradient has a component in the negative $\hat{x}$-direction. Thus, our pressure gradient is "toward the back" and "down".
:::

Now we can go back to our observation about the pressure gradient at the surface: it must be parallel to the surface normal. Same result as above: the liquid climbs the back wall.

We can also recognize that the higher pressure toward the back corresponds to a greater depth below the (locally higher) free surface: $p \sim \rho g h$, with $h$ measured down from the tilted surface right above it, exactly like ordinary hydrostatics.

<!-- Just for practice moving between coordinate system, let's see what this looks like set up in cylindrical coordinates centered on the tank, with $\theta=0$ along $\hat x$.

The components of Newton's second law in cylindrical coordinates are

$$
\begin{align*}
    \rho a_r &= -\pd{p}{r}\\
    \rho a_\theta &= -\frac{1}{r}\pd{p}{\theta}\\
    \rho a_y &= -\pd{p}{y}-\rho g
\end{align*}
$$

Here's the wrinkle that made us switch to Cartesian above: the vehicle's acceleration $\mathbf a = a\hat x$ is one fixed vector, but $\hat r$ and $\hat\theta$ *rotate* with $\theta$. Resolving $\mathbf a$ onto the local $\hat r,\hat\theta$ at a given point gives

$$
a_r = \mathbf a\cdot\hat r = a\cos\theta, \qquad a_\theta = \mathbf a \cdot \hat\theta = -a\sin\theta.
$$

Neither is a constant, and $a_\theta$ isn't zero — both depend on where you are around the tank. (Contrast this with true rigid-body *rotation*, where $a_r=-\Omega^2 r$ and $a_\theta=0$ hold at *every* $\theta$ — that's the case where "cylindrical, axisymmetric, ignore $\theta$" is exactly right, not just a convenient approximation along one ray.)

Plugging in and integrating the same way as before gives

$$
p(r,\theta,y) = -\rho a\, r\cos\theta - \rho g y + \text{constant} = -\rho a x - \rho g y + \text{constant},
$$

using $x=r\cos\theta$ — the same pressure field as the Cartesian solution, as it must be. Setting $p=0$ for the free surface:

$$
y = -\frac{a}{g}\, r\cos\theta.
$$

This is the same tilted plane, just written in cylindrical coordinates — a genuine two-dimensional surface, not a function of $r$ alone. Slicing it at $\theta=0$ recovers $y=-(a/g)r$, which is the tempting (but only locally-true) formula you'd get if you assumed $a_r=a$ everywhere instead of $a\cos\theta$. -->
